paragraphs: When the ice broke on the Ba River, the camel caravans from Hexi arrived in Chang’an.

The bells on their harnesses rang across Ba Bridge and into the spring mud. The felt-wrapped packs still carried dust from Guzang, and the camel drivers hawked grape wine in halting Guanzhong speech. When a jar was opened, its sweetness drifted halfway down the street. Chang’an men buying wine asked first the price, then how many battles had been fought in the west. What did a tavern keeper know? He took a few remarks overheard from soldiers and made them into a great victory, picked several names from among the dead and bestowed on them exploits worthy of a hundred men apiece. At the liveliest part of the tale, several tables cheered together.

Only an old veteran near the West Market gate, missing two fingers, had had enough. He turned his bowl upside down and said that many who died on the Liangzhou road would never even have their bones brought home. Where had the tavern keeper found so many glorious adventures?

The drinkers argued with him. Had General Murong defeated the men of Dai? Yes, said the veteran. Had Great Qin gained another province? Yes. Then why sour a happy occasion? The man rubbed the old callus at the stumps of his fingers and was silent for a long while. “My son’s reward still hasn’t come from the Department of State Affairs.”

Spring filled Chang’an in the third month. Peach blossoms opened within the palace walls and beyond the city ramparts where countless soldiers had been buried. Trees knew nothing of who had conquered the land. They flowered every year all the same.

Inside the Department of State Affairs, however, there was scarcely a moment’s peace. Registers of military merit had arrived twice from Guzang and northern Dai. For five nights the clerks kept their lamps burning, matching every dead man’s name, home district and rank against the granary charged with issuing his family’s grain. Murong Chui’s reports from the frontier recorded achievements differently from the old practice. The final pages named men who had repaired carts, raised ramparts and carried the wounded. Fu Agui, killed in the battle on the snowy plain, was no longer entered merely as “one Di soldier.” The ward where his parents lived, and the granary responsible for their grain, were recorded as well.
Fu Hong sat beneath the window and listened to the departments quarrel for an entire morning.

An old officer of the Military Bureau struck the table with the shaft of his brush. “If the craftsmen who mend siege carts receive merit, what about the men who cook for the camp? At this rate we’ll be paying rewards all the way from Chang’an to Guzang.”
“A sound battering cart breaks a gate; a broken one crushes a man,” said a young registrar, raising his head. “Wasn’t the skin on that craftsman’s hands worn away in the army too?”

The old officer was about to answer when another clerk pushed a register between them. “Leave that for now. Fu Shao and Liang Aguo have both claimed credit for closing the same breach in the wagon formation. Two witnesses in camp give opposing accounts. Whose name goes first?”

Fu Hong did not put brush to paper at once. He remembered his first visit to this office after Wang Meng’s death, when he could not explain even a single extra name on the muster rolls. The books had grown thicker since then; behind many of the names he could almost see the men themselves. He ordered the medical records brought out. Fu Shao had been wounded in the arm, Liang Aguo in the shoulder. Their positions had been no more than seven paces apart, and both wounds had been suffered before the wagons closed ranks.
“Enter them together,” he said. “There is no need to rank one man’s merit above the other. Record the particulars fully. If the award is challenged one day, at least we shall know who saw what.”

The old officer sighed and obeyed. Watching him copy the entries, Fu Hong suddenly asked about Fu Agui’s family. After searching two registers, the clerk found a tiny circle of vermilion. The relief payment had long since been approved, but the money and grain were still on the road; no official had yet signed for their escort.
“Send someone after it,” Fu Hong said. “The spring planting won’t wait for an imperial decree.”

That afternoon Fu Rong entered the office with an urgent dispatch from Beidi. The Duke of Beihai, Fu Luo, had returned to the capital with three hundred personal guards. Seventeen commanders who had once served beneath him had also taken lodgings at the relay hostel.
“His Majesty has invited him to the spring banquet,” Fu Rong said. “Only Fu Luo himself will be admitted to the inner tables.”
“Does my royal uncle know the order of seating?” Fu Hong asked.

“What difference would knowing make?” Fu Rong unfolded the newly prepared seating register. His eyes paused at one entry. “Murong Chui is still in the northern marches, yet his empty place stands at the head of the generals. Do you suppose Fu Luo will fail to notice?”
“The places are assigned for merit in this campaign. We cannot give the seats of those who fought to men who did not go.”

“I never said the order was wrong.” Fu Rong closed the register. “Move a man an inch and he thinks you have shifted his ancestors’ graves an inch as well. Fu Luo has held the frontier for years. Every winter his old followers still send cattle and wine to his house. Now they must collect their rations from the Department of State Affairs. Of course some resent it.”
“More than three thousand men are still missing from Beidi’s military rolls.”
Fu Rong looked up. “Are the soldiers missing, or merely the paper on which they were entered?”
Fu Hong had no answer. His uncle did not press him. “Investigate. A man may lose face at a spring banquet. On the frontier, if soldiers go missing, lives are at stake.”

On the ninth day of the third month, lamps were lit throughout Weiyang Palace. The newly planted peach trees before the hall had not yet put down firm roots. A gust carried their pink petals into the palace watercourse. Musicians tested their strings behind a screen; before the music began, the clatter of cups and dishes had filled the air. An envoy from Hexi glanced at the gilded pillars and rubbed the sand from his boots on a felt mat. Several imperial kinsmen were already seated inside, recounting their old northern campaigns with that easy closeness known only to men who had shared a battlefield.

The place of honor among the generals on the eastern side stood empty. A newly forged sword and a golden wine cup lay before it. The sword hilt caught the lamplight and shone brighter at a distance than the jewels about the hall. Murong Chui had not come home, but his renown had arrived ahead of him.

Fu Luo entered without the flush of wine or any open sign of anger. His court robe was black; the hard bones of his shoulders stood out beneath the cloth, and an old scar above his brow emerged from the shifting light. Years of frontier winds had cut deep lines beside his temples. He returned the greetings of the imperial household one by one. Only when he reached his own place did his steps slow.
“Whose seat is that?” he asked, pointing to the empty place.
“Champion General Murong Chui’s,” the attendant murmured.
“And where is he?”
“Still on the frontier.”
Fu Luo looked again at the arrangement. “Very good. Even an empty stool outranks me now.”

Fu Rong came forward to guide him to his place. He spoke mildly, asking him to spare some dignity for those being honored today. Fu Luo listened to the end, then asked, “Where was Murong Chui while I was defending Beidi?”
“In the state of Yan,” Fu Rong answered.
“And his men were fighting whom?”
Fu Rong met his eyes. “The wars of former years have their own accounts to settle.”

Fu Luo gave a cold laugh. At that moment Fu Hong approached, bowed as a junior to his uncle, and explained that today’s arrangement honored the present campaign alone. It did not erase earlier service on the northern frontier.
“You have learned to speak this way too,” Fu Luo said, studying him. “Then tell me which register contains the soldiers I buried along the border.”
“The Department of State Affairs keeps the old records of those whose names can still be traced.”
“And those whose names cannot?”
Fu Hong fell silent. Fu Luo did not pursue the question. He merely straightened the seal of the Duke of Beihai at his waist and stood waiting for the emperor.
The bell struck three times. Fu Jian entered the hall. He saw that Fu Luo was still standing, then looked at the empty seat before the generals. He paused, and understood.
“Fu Luo.” He used his cousin’s name, not his title. “After all these years out in the Beidi wind, will you refuse even to sit down when you come back to Chang’an?”
Fu Luo bowed low. When he straightened, he said, “Your servant wishes only to ask whether today we celebrate merit, or show the Fu clan who is now permitted to sit above whom.”
The musicians stopped playing. Incense rose in a thin ribbon before the throne. The hall grew so still that the brush of a sleeve against a mat could be heard.
Fu Jian called for the seating register, turned two pages, and asked, “How many of your men took part in the fighting at Guzang and in northern Dai?”
“My men were holding the passes of Beidi.”

“There are other provisions for rewarding men who guard the passes. Today we honor soldiers who have returned, though some of their comrades never will. If you come to plead for those men, I shall listen. If all you want is a seat, I will not change the order.”

The corner of Fu Luo’s eye twitched. “I have never fought for a seat alone. Those who marched beside Your Majesty in former years must now report to Chang’an even the handful of guards they take with them. The seals of our princely fiefs remain, while command of our soldiers has been scattered to the winds. Murong Chui wins merit today and is called a general. I won merit in years past and have nothing left but a title.”
“How many soldiers do you want?” Fu Jian asked.
“I want Your Majesty to remember that Beidi was not held with empty decrees.”

Fu Jian rose and descended slowly from the dais. As young men he and Fu Luo had shared a tent, and he had listened to his cousin sharpening his blade through snowy nights. Now they had to stand apart in the hall, separated by the rites of sovereign and subject.

“I remember,” Fu Jian said. “The passes you defended, the men who died there: the court will not erase them. But the soldiers who went beyond the frontier with you drew Qin rations, and their wives and children live on Qin soil. Because you feel slighted today, must their descendants inherit your grievance for generations?”
Fu Luo advanced half a pace. “The Qin of which Your Majesty speaks: whose Qin is it?”

The words fell among the cups like a piece of cold iron. Some of the imperial kinsmen lowered their eyes; others tightened their grip on their goblets. Even the courtiers who could ordinarily smooth over any quarrel dared not speak.
Fu Jian gazed at his cousin. “The Fu clan conquered this realm. I have never denied it.”

Fu Luo’s expression eased slightly. Fu Jian continued, “So the descendants of the late ruler’s followers receive honors, land and stipends. The wives and children of those who die for the state must be fed and clothed. But if every army becomes a private inheritance, with what shall Great Qin defend the realm that comes after us?”

“Your Majesty may gather every soldier under the court,” Fu Luo replied, “yet leave the throne to the crown prince. I dare ask only this: if the Fu clan’s achievements cannot be inherited as military power, why should Fu blood alone inherit the world?”
The question struck so hard that even Fu Hong raised his head.

Fu Jian did not hide behind a shout of anger. After a silence he said, “That my son will succeed me is the law of Qin as it stands today. I hope he will guard the realm well. I would not dare promise that a thousand years to come will know no calamity. Fu Hong.”
“Your son is here.”

“Remember what your royal uncle has asked today. If a time comes when all you possess is the claim of father and son, and you cannot protect the realm, do not expect your name to defend its cities for you.”

Fu Hong bowed his head in obedience. Fu Luo felt colder still. The emperor had openly acknowledged that the throne remained within the Fu family, yet that admission left Fu Luo nowhere to press his claim to troops. His cousin spoke without shame of a realm inherited by one house, and with the same frankness demanded that the imperial kinsmen accept restraint.
Fu Rong invited Fu Luo to sit. Fu Luo set the cup before him straight, and at last ceased resisting.
The strings and flutes began again. The first melody, however, faltered on a wrong note, and the musician hurried to adjust his strings. No one laughed.

Before long Fu Shao and Liang Aguo, honored for their service in northern Dai, were led into the hall. They were still bickering as they came. The bandage had only recently been removed from Fu Shao’s left arm, and he held his cup awkwardly. Liang Aguo’s injured shoulder made his gait uneven; when Fu Shao walked too quickly, he cursed him for trying to drive a man to his death.

Fu Jian asked which of them had closed the breach in the wagon formation on the snowfield. Fu Shao said he had led the men there first. Liang Aguo retorted that without him holding the gap, Fu Shao would merely have charged into a heap of dead horses. At last someone in the hall laughed. Fu Jian heard them out, ordered silk rewards for both, and asked whether Fu Agui, killed in the battle, had family.

A registrar stepped forward with a ledger. Fu Agui’s aged mother lived north of the Wei River, he said, and her sight had lately grown dim. Her district granary had dispatched the first allotment of relief grain, but the remainder still awaited certification along the road. Fu Jian ordered a review within a fixed number of days, and commanded that Fu Agui’s wooden identification tablet be delivered to his mother.

At that, Liang Aguo ceased smiling. On the snowfield he had heard Helan Wu answer the roll call in the dead Fu Agui’s place, and he could still hear that single response. Fu Shao lowered his eyes to the wine cup that his hands were still strong enough to hold. Suddenly he did not know how to offer his thanks.

The banquet went on. Craftsmen, scouts and officers who had transported wounded soldiers came forward in turn to receive their honors. Several young men of the imperial clan watched with resentment on their faces, but none spoke again. Fu Luo never touched his grape wine. His gaze returned again and again to Murong Chui’s empty seat, then drifted to a peach tree outside the hall whose blossoms had already begun to fall. He remembered the fires in the frontier watchtowers of his youth. There had been no golden cups there. They had passed wine in half a cattle horn, and the brothers buried in the snow had not even received official ranks upon their grave markers.

As the sun declined, the officials dispersed. At the palace gate the new wooden desk for checking command tokens still stood in place. Everyone leaving had to be identified against the list. Fu Luo presented the seal and travel tally of the Duke of Beihai. The guard commander knew him perfectly well, yet still ordered a clerk to examine the entry carefully.
“Afraid I’m pretending to be myself?” Fu Luo asked.
The commander went pale. “It is an order of the Right Guard General, my lord. I beg Your Lordship’s forgiveness.”
A voice came from the shadows beneath the palace wall. “Do not blame him, Your Lordship. So many people have come and gone today; the gatekeepers fear making a mistake.”

Yao Chang emerged from beneath the colonnade with his customary smile. At the banquet he had sat well toward the rear, possessing neither a victorious general’s sword nor an imperial kinsman’s grievance. When the guests departed he looked like any ordinary officer who had been on duty overnight.
Fu Luo took back his tally. “General Yao certainly keeps disciplined soldiers.”
“Even I must surrender my token for inspection at the palace gate,” Yao Chang said with a smile. “Once I forgot it and stood outside for a full half hour.”
Fu Luo looked at him. “At least you may still come and go through the palace gates. You are better off than I.”

Yao Chang let the remark pass. He walked beside Fu Luo as far as the willows and asked how the spring grass was coming on in Beidi. Fu Luo said the winter snow had been heavy, the horses had grown painfully thin, and the grain registers of more than three thousand men in the old garrisons remained unsettled. Yao Chang offered a few words of sympathy, then said, after a while, “There are few in Chang’an who understand the frontier. Your Lordship came back and spoke truths that were hard to hear, and His Majesty listened in the end. Men who came to Qin as its former enemies have no such bond.”
“You said nothing today. Yet you seem to have understood everything.”

Yao Chang laughed softly. “And what use is understanding? Once I had followers of my own; when I rode out, men held my horse. Now an imperial decree has placed the Right Guard under my command, but to change the guards at a single palace gate I need seals from half the offices in the capital. There is one advantage: when trouble comes, the blame cannot all be laid upon me.”
Fu Luo asked abruptly, “Do you think His Majesty will always listen to me?”
Yao Chang glanced at the receding palace gate before answering with care. “Your Lordship is of the imperial blood. As for affairs of the army, I would not presume to judge.”
“Cautious as ever.”

“An elder among the Qiang once told me: when snow hides the mountains, first listen to whether your horse can still walk,” Yao Chang said. “In Beidi, the frontier must be held in fact. If trouble comes at the passes, His Majesty will have to ask those who defend them.”
It might have been consolation. It might have been a warning. Fu Luo looked back at the willow branches moving in the wind and said nothing for a long while. Yao Chang bowed and took his leave.

Fu Luo’s guards led up his horse. As the Duke of Beihai mounted, an old memory returned. Years before, he had come back to Chang’an with a dozen men covered in blood. Fu Jian had met him outside the palace gates and handed him a jug of hot wine before he could even take off his armor. In those days the guards had only to see him from afar to open the gates.
Now the gates still opened, and men still called him lord. But first they had to read the line bearing his name.

His old army in Beidi was waiting for him. Fu Luo gathered the reins and rode into the dusk of the long avenue. Peach petals crushed beneath his horse’s iron shoes clung to the metal, and had not fallen away even after he had ridden far.
